486.4   Order restricting
publication — sexual offences.
—(1)   Subject
to subsection (2), the presiding judge or justice may make an order directing

be published in any document or broadcast or transmitted in any way, in proceedings
in respect of

(
a
)    any of the
following offences:

(i)    an offence
under section 151, 152, 153, 153.1, 155, 159, 160, 162, 163.1, 170, 171, 172,

347,

under section 144 (rape), 145 (attempt to commit rape), 149 (indecent assault
on female), 156 (indecent assault on male) or 245 (common assault) or subsection
246(1) (assault with intent) of the
Criminal Code
,
chapter C-34
of the
Revised Statutes of Canada, 1970, as it read immediately before January 4, 1983,
or

(iii)    an offence
under subsection 146(1) (sexual intercourse with a female under 14) or (2)
(sexual intercourse with a female between 14 and 16) or section 151 (seduction

Criminal

chapter C-34

(
b

referred to in any of subparagraphs (
a
)(i) to (iii).

(2)
Mandatory order on
application.
—   In proceedings in respect of the offences
referred to in paragraph (1)(
a
) or (
b
), the presiding judge or
justice shall

(
a
)    at the first
reasonable opportunity, inform any witness under the age of eighteen years and
the complainant of the right to make an application for the order; and

(
b
)    on application
made by the complainant, the prosecutor or any such witness, make the order.

.   .   .

486.6   Offence.
—(1)   Every person who fails to comply with an order
made under
subsection 486.4(1)
, (2) or (3) or 486.5(1) or (2) is guilty of an
offence punishable on summary conviction.

I.

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

Mr. B.M. pleaded guilty on May 6, 2008
[1]
to three counts of
Indecent Assault on a Female Person contrary to
s. 149
of the
Criminal Code of
Canada
[2]
,
committed during the time period between October 12, 1972 and December 31,
1974. The three victims are sisters, and the accused is their uncle.  An Agreed
Statement of Facts was filed with respect to two of the three victims, E.S and
E.M.

[
2
]

Although the accused pleaded guilty to
indecently assaulting M.L.C., he did not agree to a set of facts concerning
her.

[
3
]

The accused pleaded not guilty to a charge

s.146
(1)
of the
Criminal Code of Canada
[3]
.

[
4
]

The trial of an issue was held regarding
that count, and the circumstances generally of any assault on M.L.C.

[
5
]

Evidence was heard on May 6, 2008.  The
accused was found guilty of the indecent assault on E.S. and E.M., consequent

evidence differs in many respects, including the number of acts, their
frequency and the surrounding circumstances. The accused denies he had
intercourse at any time with M.L.C.

[
6
]

Thereafter submissions were made on a number
of days on the factual issues, the legal issue of Similar Act, and sentencing
submissions.

[
7
]

This is a very difficult sentencing case.
The Court is in debt to both counsel, who were most thorough in their
submissions and presentation of the case. I have extensively reviewed all of
the materials which they provided. If I fail to mention a particular submission
or document presented, suffice to say that I have considered all of them.

II.

FACTS

A.

Agreed Statement of Facts

[
8
]

An Agreed Statement of Facts was filed as an
Exhibit on the plea
[4]
.

Background

[
9
]

E.M., E.S. and M.L.C. are sisters and are
all victims in this occurrence.  On Monday, September 18, 2006 they attended
the Special Victims Unit of Peel Regional Police in relation to a complaint of

disclosed the following information.

[
10
]

The offences against the victims occurred

that she was between 10 and 11 years of age, and M.L.C. believed that she was
between 7 and 9 years of age at the time of the offences.

[
11
]

During this time period, all three victims
lived with their parents and their brother at an address on D[…] Street in
Toronto.  On occasion, the victims would attend the resi-

dence of the accused, B.M., by
themselves. Mr. B.M. is an uncle of the victims by marriage.  At the time of
the offences, Mr. B.M. lived at W[…] Road in the Clarkson area of Mississauga
with his wife L.M. and his children S.[1] and S.[2].

INCIDENTS/INVESTIGATION

[
12
]

E. S. reported three incidents involving the

[

B.
Gardiner Hearing Evidence

[

Both the Crown and the Defence called

Gardiner Hearing
[5]

The burden of proof rests upon the Crown to establish any disputed aggravating
circumstance(s) beyond a reasonable doubt.

[

In this case, Mr. B.M. disputes the

[

M.L.C., although it is not disputed that she was under the age of 14 years at

B.

[
23
]

The Crown called M.L.C., E.M., and E.S. to

M.L.C

[
24

M.L.C.  is the youngest sister, and grew up

: 'society,
through the courts, must show its abhorrence of particular types of crime, and
the only way in which courts can show this is by the sentences they pass.' The

negative penalties designed to prevent [harm[ by increasing the cost [to] the offender…

Advanced age is usually a mitigating factor …[because]
the older a person is, the harder it is to serve a prison term and the less is
that person's life expectancy after prison. As a general rule, however,
advanced age does not entitle a person who has committed an offence of the kind
we are dealing with here to a non-incarceratory sentence. The most such an
offender can hope for is a reduction in the time he or she would otherwise have
served…
An accused's infirmity, always a factor to be considered, may
warrant a reduction in the sentence that would otherwise have been imposed or a
different kind of sentence. It all depends on the nature of the infirmity and
the nature and seriousness of the crime.
Compassion must neither be stifled
nor allowed to take control.

Another case considering the frailty of the
offender is

R. v
Oziel
,
[1997] O.J. No. 1185 (C.A.)
.In that case, a
sixty year old offender had underwent quadruple heart bypass surgery since the
imposition of sentence. The Court of Appeal stated at para. 12:

The offences took place a long time ago and the trial
judge accepted that the appellant was no longer a present danger to the public
and that there was no need to consider specific deterrence.  The
appellant has been ostracized within the Jewish community. The trial judge's
sentence was imposed on the basis of general deterrence and denunciation.
While
we are of the opinion that these are important considerations, we feel that a
sentence must also reflect the particular circumstances of the
individual.  Having regard to the precarious state of the appellant's
health, a fit and proper sentence in the exceptional circumstances of this case
is the minimum penitentiary sentence.
Accordingly, we would
grant leave to appeal the sentence, allow the appeal as to sentence and
substitute a sentence of two years.

[
178
]

A penitentiary sentence is the only
appropriate sentence in this case. A conditional sentence is therefore not
possible, as the preconditions in s. 742.1 are not engaged.

[
179
]

The overall range of sentence for the s. 146
(1) offence in these circumstances is submitted to be three to five years.
Weighing all of the circumstances including the mitigating factors here, the
submission for a sentence of three years on that count is fit.

[
180

The Court does not diminish the significance
of the sentences on the indecent assault counts involving three young victims.
The sentence should be consecutive. However, the
totality principle, in short, requires a sentencing judge who orders an offender
to serve consecutive sentences for multiple offences to ensure that the
cumulative sentence rendered does not exceed the overall culpability of the
offender.  “A cumulative sentence may offend the totality principle if the
aggregate sentence is substantially above the normal level of a sentence for
the most serious of the individual sentences involved.”
[13]

[
181

For the above reason, although each of the
three counts pursuant to
s. 149

these sentences to run concurrent to each other, but consecutive to the other
count pursuant to
s.146(1)
